column1: # .github/auth-register.tsv — one canonical authentication method per cell,
# and every second method that is allowed to exist alongside it.
# Rows are written BY HAND. Recompute fingerprints and line numbers with:
# The rule, the four conditions a justification must meet, the anchor forms
# and what the gate fails on: scripts/auth-register.sh
# revisit: a CHECKABLE FACT. A date is never a trigger, and the gate says so.
# anchor: go:<path>#<Symbol> | text:<path>#<literal> | none: (needs a cite)
# 'line' is navigation only and is refreshed each run; it is NOT part of the
# fingerprint, so edits above a row do not churn this file. Editing the
# ANCHORED declaration does change the fingerprint, and the gate then fails
# until someone re-reads the row against the code that changed.
# This file is PUBLIC. A row describing a fail-open that is unfixed and
# reachable does not belong here; it lives in a private geekdojo-brain issue
# and moves here in the pull request that fixes it.

column5: A discoverable passkey issues an opaque session. The session token is stored as its sha256 hash, and user verification is required.
One normalized origin allowlist feeds WebAuthn, CORS, the WebSocket origin check and cross-origin protection. The security header set ships with it and carries no HSTS.
One fail-closed first-run predicate. A read error is an error, never the answer 'no users yet'.

column5: A join token bound to the node id and to the role at mint, re-read on every connect. A token carrying no role never validates.

column4: node to control plane, server auth, NATS
column5: The bus key's SPKI pin. One resolver reads it, in order, from the seeded environment value, from the pin file a delivery wrote, and — on the controlplane's own agent alone — from the pin file its api writes at every start. A pin that was configured and is not usable never falls through to plaintext: the node refuses to dial rather than send its join token in the clear. A node that was never given a pin still dials plaintext, which is how a fleet enrolled before the pin existed receives one.

One fact revokes: the token row is revoked, or the node is removed. Today that revokes the token and closes every live bus session it authenticated, and the node stays in inventory so its records remain analysable. Widening the cascade to HTTPS, the tailnet and the leaf files is tracked, not done.
None. The api reads alert state from VictoriaMetrics in a background loop; there is no inbound callback to authenticate.

Every secret file is written 0600 through a synced temporary file and a rename, with the mode set by fchmod rather than inherited from a umask. Modes are per file and no unit sets a UMask. One helper per Go module owns that decision (E36).
artifactsig verification for an explicit purpose, with the purpose OID fixed per artifact class.
One Go validator for the operator public key, shared by every surface that accepts one.

column4: human trust in the mesh CA, out of band
column5: Trust on first use, for every device. There is no fingerprint comparison surface.
One version-admission gate for the OS, the firewall and the catalog. No downgrade override.

One verifier resolved from the trust root, with no permissive mode to select. Construction never returns an error, so there is no error path a caller can mishandle back into permissiveness: an absent, unreadable or unparseable root yields an unavailable verifier that refuses every artifact and carries the reason.

One pinned-TLS helper, with one typed pin: the SHA-256 of the DER SubjectPublicKeyInfo, in the same encoding as the bus pin. Verification runs in VerifyConnection, so it also runs on a resumed connection. There is no unpinned mode and no http endpoint.
One custody check, gated by an authenticated session.
column6: Phase 1 of restore runs with no session.
column7: Before a restore there is no user row, so there is nobody to authenticate. The first-run predicate is the only gate that exists at that point.
column9: A surface exists that can authenticate the operator before any user row exists.

column5: One mint function.
column6: Two profiles, one for a node and one for a user device.
column7: A node key is single-use, carries the node tag and is expired when the enrol step ends. A user key carries the user-device tag, refuses node tags, is capped and is shown once. The two differ in every field that decides authority.
column9: Node and user devices are admitted with the same tag set and the same lifecycle.

column5: One key per trust root.
column6: The control plane holds two, the bus key and the mesh CA.
column7: They root different things and are presented to different verifiers. Merging them would make one compromise reach both the bus and every browser that trusts the mesh CA.
column9: The bus and the mesh are verified against one trust root.

column4: node to control plane, client auth, NATS
column5: A credential ends when a fact ends it, and revoke forces the disconnect.
column6: The minted connection credential also lapses after 24 hours.
column7: The lapse covers a missed forced disconnect. On reconnect the client re-presents its token and the registry is read again, so the bound is a safety net that re-checks a fact rather than a clock that decides one.
column9: Revoke confirms every session drop, so a missed disconnect becomes a detectable fact.

column4: agent to control plane, backup transfer, HTTPS
column5: The transfer grant is valid while the operation is open.
column6: The grant also carries a lifetime.
column7: The lifetime is derived from the operation's own work budget plus slack, and covers an operation that ends without closing its grant.
column9: An operation that ends always emits the fact that closes its grant.

column4: device to mesh admission, node profile
column5: The node key is expired explicitly when the enrol step ends, on success or failure.
column6: The key also carries a 10-minute expiry.
column7: It covers an api that stops mid-step, when nothing is left running to issue the explicit expiry.
column9: The enrol step's end is durable across an api restart.

column4: third-party verification of our leaves, TLS
column5: A credential is ended by a fact.
column6: Application and server leaves are bounded only by their expiry.
column7: Browsers and the tailnet client verify these leaves, and Rasputin publishes no revocation list, so expiry is the only bound those verifiers can apply. A copy taken off the node stays valid to them until then.
column9: Rasputin publishes a revocation list those verifiers consult.

column4: join token mint, out of band
column5: One mint path.
column6: The seed is minted two ways: offline for a matched set, or online through the add-node flow under a session.
column7: The offline path has to work with no control plane reachable at all. The online path has to bind a node id the operator chose in the interface.
column9: One path can mint a seed both offline and under a session.

column5: One custody key-derivation resolver.
column6: Two derivations: a memory-hard one for a human passphrase, a fast one for a generated recovery code.
column7: The cost parameter follows the secret's entropy. A full-entropy generated code gains nothing from a memory-hard derivation, and a human-chosen passphrase needs one.
column9: The recovery code and the passphrase carry the same entropy.

column5: One admin channel.
column6: A container exec to the local socket is kept, used only to mint a short-lived REST key at each api start.
column7: The mesh server has no way to issue the first REST key over REST.
column9: The mesh server can issue an initial API key without local socket access.

column4: platform sidecar to host, unix socket
column5: A client is given a scoped credential for the service it talks to.
column6: The container socket is mounted into the collector sidecar.
column7: The collector's container discovery has no scoped equivalent in the daemon's API.
column9: The collector can discover containers with a scoped credential.

column5: One apply sink and one key path.
column6: The OS and the firewall differ in both.
column7: The firewall's root filesystem is a read-only squashfs and its configuration sink is UCI and procd, not an env file and systemd. Neither difference is a choice.
column9: The firewall image carries a writable root filesystem and a systemd sink.

column5: A detached CMS signature.
column6: The A/B update bundle carries its signature inside the bundle.
column7: The bundle format embeds the signature and the updater verifies it with its own keyring before we see the payload.
column9: The bundle format accepts a detached signature.

column5: One signing credential.
column6: There are two, one for releases and one for the catalog.
column7: Separating them is what makes the purpose OIDs enforceable: a catalog leaf cannot sign a release and a release leaf cannot sign a catalog.
column9: One credential can carry both purposes without either being able to sign the other's artifacts.

column5: Every field of a release selection comes from the verified manifest.
column6: The channel comes from an unsigned flag.
column7: The prerelease flag is a property of the hosting platform's release object, not of the signed manifest. A signed channel value may only narrow it.
column9: The manifest carries a signed channel value.

column5: A session ended by facts: logout, sign-out-others, deleting the passkey.
column6: A 7-day absolute lifetime also ends it.
column7: A lost or retired laptop produces no fact the api can observe, so no checkable fact is available to end that session. This is the one credential bound here with nothing behind it.
column9: A signed-in device emits a fact the api can observe when it is lost or retired.

column5: One verifier implementation.
column6: The laptop side is a shell check rather than the Go verifier.
column7: No Rasputin binary exists on the laptop at first flash. The laptop has openssl and nothing else we ship.
column9: A signed verifier binary is distributed with the flasher.

column5: One publisher trust root.
column6: The firewall image keeps the upstream distribution's feed signing keys.
column7: Conditional, and only while the package manager is kept. Rasputin never installs a package at runtime; only an operator does.
column9: The firewall image ships without a package manager.

column5: Every input to a trust decision is authenticated.
column6: Time is taken from unauthenticated NTP.
column7: No authenticated time source is available to an appliance on an arbitrary LAN with no operator configuration. What is narrowed instead is how much depends on the clock.
column9: An authenticated time source is available with no operator configuration.

column5: A credential is authorized by a checkable fact.
column6: The seed's authority is physical possession of the medium it arrives on.
column7: Nothing exists on a node before the seed that could authenticate it, so possession is the only fact available at that point.
column9: A node can authenticate a seed before it holds any credential.

column5: One helper decides the mode of every file a process writes.
column6: The api and the agent each carry their own copy of that helper.
column7: The api's package is internal to a different Go module, so the agent binary cannot import it at all. The copy keeps the same semantics for every name both packages share and carries only what the agent uses.
column9: The helper lives in a module both binaries already import.

column5: Every field of a release selection comes from a manifest this api verified against the trust root for the release purpose.
column6: A release below its component's version floor is resolved WITHOUT reading its signature, so its version, asset names and checksums are taken on HTTPS alone.
column7: Releases published before the release purpose OID existed are signed by a leaf that carries no extendedKeyUsage at all, which the verifier refuses by construction. Measured, not assumed: rasputin-os 2026.08.3 and earlier are signed by `Rasputin Release Leaf 001` (no EKU); 2026.08.4 onward by `Rasputin Bundle Signing leaf-003`, which carries the release OID. Requiring verification below the floor would leave a cluster still running one of those releases unable to resolve the flashable image for its OWN version, so it could not add a node at all -- turning a stale-version problem into an onboarding outage. The narrowest difference this forces is per component and per version: at or above the floor a signature is REQUIRED and a missing one is a hard failure, so the exception cannot be used to downgrade a signed release by deleting its .sig.
column9: No supported release predates its component's floor.

column4: human trust in the mesh CA, out of band
column5: A trust anchor is verified against a surface the person already trusts.
column6: No device verifies the mesh CA out of band; every device takes it on first use.
column7: Recorded decision. A fingerprint comparison surface was considered and not taken, because it adds a step to every device for a value the operator cannot check independently.
column9: The provisioning tool mints the mesh CA for a matched set and the preseed carries a first-run claim code.

column4: browser to api, pending ceremony, memory
column5: The pending ceremony is consumed when the ceremony finishes.
column6: A 5-minute bound also ends it.
column7: An abandoned ceremony produces no fact the api could observe. The bound frees the memory and ends a stale ceremony's authority; it is a safety net, not a state transition.
column9: An abandoned ceremony emits a fact the api can observe.

column4: node to control plane, client auth
column5: One credential authenticates the node to the control plane.
column6: NATS authenticates with the join token; HTTPS authenticates with a separately registered key.
column7: Recorded decisions: mutual TLS was put out of scope on the bus, and a persisted signing key for node identity was superseded. The HTTPS side must not carry the long-lived join token as a bearer.
column9: Every known cluster reports the enforced bus mode, at which point the callout can accept the registered key and NATS keeps the token only for first registration.

column4: collector to api, server auth, HTTPS
column5: The collector trusts the api's bus certificate by exact bytes.
column6: The collector trusts the mesh chain instead.
column7: Conditional. It applies only if the collector cannot be given an exact-bytes trust anchor and a self-signed client certificate.
column9: The probe runs the pinned collector image against an exact-bytes anchor. If it is accepted, this row is deleted.

column4: node process to mesh, server trust, HTTPS
column5: A process is given its trust root through its own configuration.
column6: The tailnet client is given the mesh CA through an environment variable.
column7: That variable is the only hook the client's runtime offers for a per-process trust root; it exposes no configuration option for one.
column9: The tailnet client exposes a configuration option for its trust root.
